To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the introduction of a 2-oxo substituent into the 13-position of the PG skeleton, and of a 1-amino or 1-acylamino substituent into the side chain, leads to compounds that are potent, competitive antagonists of PGs in vitro and in intact animals.
the 7-amino-7-deoxy-13-prostaglandin derivatives are potent antagonists of PGF2a and PGl2.
amide and l-amine derivatives of F prost-landins are potent and competitive prostaglandin (PG) antagonists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of amides and l-amino acid derivatives of F prostanoic acid (FPA) (1), the precursor of the F PGs, and their evaluation as PG antagonists.
the preparation and biological evaluation of amide and l-ammino derivatives of F prostanoic and prostanoic acids.
the development of PG antagonists based upon the 7-oxo prostaglandin analogs (7-oxa PGs).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the compounds described here are the most potent, specific and competitive PG antagonists yet reported.
these compounds are potent and specific PG antagonists, which inhibit the action of PGs in vitro and in intact animals, and are not PG mimics.
the compounds described here are potent and specific inhibitors of PG biosynthesis and function in a variety of systems, and they are useful for the elucidation of the roles of PGs in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PGs are antagonized by the l-amino derivatives (I) of the PGs and by the amides (II) of PGs, and that the l-amino- and amide-derivatives of PGF2a are the most potent antagonists.
a simple amide derivative of F prostaglanding, namely, F2a-amide, is a potent and specific antagonist of PGF2a in vitro, and a competitive antagonist of PGF in vivo.
the introduction of a carboxylic acid function at position 11 of PGs results in the formation of potent antagonists which are highly specific and competitive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 15-amino group of F prostaglands is the most important site of interaction with PG receptors, and that the 15-carboxylate is the most critical functional group for receptor binding.
the amide and l-amine derivatives of PGs are potent and selective PG antagonists in vivo.
the PGs can be antagonized by amide and l-amido derivatives of the prostaglandin molecule.
